04 · Decision brief

Three findings that matter

These conclusions apply to the 30-space sample, not every Harvard study location.

01

Good spaces specialize.

Quiet carrels and reading rooms lead for focus; rooms with displays and whiteboards rise for group or presentation work. One universal ranking would conceal that trade-off.

02

Published metadata is uneven.

Only some space cards list accessibility, charging, quiet designation, or reservability. Students cannot tell whether a missing label means “unavailable” or simply “undocumented.”

03

Late access is concentrated.

Cabot and Lamont are described as 24-hour libraries, concentrating late-night choice in two buildings. Individual rooms may still have different access rules.

Recommended next moves

Make the information more decision-ready.

  1. Standardize every space card.Require the same fields for noise, power, accessibility, reservation, food, and after-hours access—and show “unknown” explicitly.
  2. Pilot live availability where demand is longest.Start with high-use, 24-hour Cabot and Lamont areas; publish room status or periodic seat-count estimates without collecting identities.
  3. Validate priorities with a short anonymous intercept survey.Ask students to rank features and record broad time blocks, avoiding names, contact details, or precise personal histories.
